Figure caption: Composition of RNC. The synthetic myeloid cell avid nucleic acid condensing RNC consisted of polymeric cores made of NAPED cross-linked succinyl-β-cyclodextrin units (each unit 16 nm in mean diameter each, ∼1500 units per core per condensing unit), resulting in an overall positive charge imparted by NAPED. Each β-CD unit is capable of host–guest interactions to (i) host various lysosomal escape agents, (ii) allows surface modification with ferrocenyl-perfluorooctylamine (FPFO), and (iii) accepts small-molecule therapeutic payloads (e.g., NF-κB stimulators). Once the cores are combined with negatively charged nucleic acid constructs, they assemble into ∼100–200 nm nanoparticles depending on the nucleic acid payload. LMP: lysosomal membrane permeabilization; NF-κB: agents affecting NF-κB signaling pathway.

Figure caption: Characterization of RNC assemblies. (A) Overview of assembly and/or condensation steps. (B) Dynamic light scattering (DLS) measurements of key compounds from (A). This particular RNC containing GFP mRNA is 138 nm in mean diameter. (C) CryoEM of different precursors shows the monodisperse nature of the NAPED cross-linked starting cores, the self-assembly into larger units upon ferrocenylation, and the further condensation with mRNA. The overall size of the RNC depends largely on the mRNA payload (see Table S1). (D) EDS mapping of a single representative RNC. F: fluorine, Fe: iron, C: carbon, O: oxygen maps. Scale bar: 100 nm.

Figure caption: Confocal imaging reveals cellular uptake and lysosomal escape. (A) Representative confocal microscopy image of macrophages (iMacs) treated with RNC (RNC741-AF647) for 18 h. Note the localization of RNC in punctuate intracellular structures, which colocalize with 10 kDa dextran-Texas Red, a prototypical lysosomal marker (D). Scale bar: 10 μm. (B) A similar image as in (A) but at 36 h shows lysosomal escape of RNC as evidenced by cytoplasmic localization of the fluorescent compound. (C) Quantification of cellular uptake of RNC as a function of dose. (E) GFP protein expression (green) of D after 18 h. Scale bar: 2 μm. (F) Colocalization (Pearson’s Correlation Coefficient Analysis) between RNC and dextran Texas red (a lysosomal marker).

Figure caption: Comparison of GFP mRNA transfection efficiency using different fluorinated RNC preparations. (A) Fluorescence microscopy images of iMACs exposed to free GFP mRNA (top) or lipofectamine-encapsulated GFP mRNA (bottom). (B) Fluorescence microscopy images of iMACs following treatment with nonfluorinated RNC constructs (top row) or fluorinated RNC (bottom row). Experiments were conducted with empty RNC (left) or different lysosomal escape agents (60 μM chloroquine, 60 μM amitriptyline, or 5 μM siramesine hydrochloride for 72 h) incorporated into a given RNC. Scale bar: 50 μm. (C) Corresponding plots of mean fluorescence intensity illustrating GFP expression. Data represent six independent replicates. Note the significant enhancement in transfection efficiency with fluorinated RNC (p < 0.0001 compared to Lipofectamine) and a further increase with LMP (p = 0.02 for RNC vs + Chloroquine). (D) Effects of different LMPs on GFP transfection efficiency. Effects were more pronounced in nonfluorinated RNC, whereas fluorinated RNC showed the highest native transfection efficiency. Across all LMP concentrations and species tested, fluorinated RNCs achieved significantly higher transfection efficiency compared to nonfluorinated RNCs (p < 0.0001).

Figure caption: Cellular toxicity of select RNC constructs. (A) FPFO-RNC with GFP mRNA (RNC741) showed no appreciable effect on cellular viability at doses used for transfection experiments. (B) Effects of increasing doses of chloroquine, amitryptyline, and siramesine incorporated into RNC741. All three LMPs showed dose-dependent cellular toxicities at effective concentrations of 100 μM (Chloroquine), 60 μM (Amitriptyline), and 15 μM (Siramesine) (n = 6). For these reasons, fluorinated RNC appears to be the preferred compound.

Figure caption: In vivo distribution following systemic injection. (A) Blood half-life following bolus IV administration in a mouse ear model shows a two-phase exponential decay with a fast component of 5 min (0.075 h) and a slow component of 40 min (0.66 h). (B) Organ distribution of fluorescently labeled RNC. Note the high uptake in tumor and lymph nodes. Scale bar: 1.5 cm. (C) Quantification of organ distribution. Expression was highest in tumor tissue. (D) Flow cytometry of RNC uptake in tumors. Note the high uptake of RNC in DC and macrophages (with expected heterogeneities among tumors). M1-M4 represent tumors grown in four different mice.
